titles.to: The Stone with the White Ring
Low Water at the Temple Stairs

replace.find: She had brought me tea for four years without once calling me miss when we were alone.
replace.with: She had brought me tea all my life, and when we were alone she seldom troubled with the miss.

replace.find: I read it four times. I unlocked my workbox
replace.with: I read it twice, and then once more. I unlocked my workbox

replace.find: Older than twenty four. I thought of the marsh road in March, the chestnuts burning his fingers,
replace.with: Older than twenty two. I thought of the wet park two springs ago, the chestnuts burning his fingers,

replace.find: Thirty years ago and still in her veil.
replace.with: Forty years ago and still in her veil.

replace.find: The first letter, soft as cloth from reading. The others in their order, tied with a faded blue thread. January. February. March.
replace.with: The first two letters, soft as cloth from reading. The others in their order, tied with a faded blue thread, every seal unbroken. Two years of months, down to March.

replace.find: The house in Half Moon Street kept its hours.
replace.with: The house off Portman Square kept its hours.

replace.find: I knew Joby Leggatt when he was short to his apron and I pay his keep now
replace.with: I knew Joby Leggatt when he was a lad in his apron and I pay his keep now

replace.find: I thought of the ironed man we fed in the scullery when I was fourteen, his ankles raw, his spoon scraping the bowl. The memory came with the taste of cold mutton fat on my tongue.
replace.with: I thought of the ironed man Hester and Joby fed at the back door when I was fourteen, the rubbed ring at his ankle, the bread going down whole. The memory came with the taste of cold bacon fat on my tongue.

replace.find: to Joby at his lodgings in Cursitor Street,
replace.with: to Joby at his lodgings over the tailor's by the Temple,

replace.find: “Since the boy was prenticed. No thanks
replace.with: “These two years, since the lawyer's letter found him at the forge. No thanks

replace.find: I was transported for forgery in twenty nine and came back
replace.with: I was transported for forgery in twenty six and came back

replace.find: The morning came soft and yellow over Half Moon Street.
replace.with: The morning came soft and yellow over Portman Square.

replace.find:
"I told you not to follow to Rochester," I said. "This is London. That is different."

He gave a short laugh that was not amusement. "You never sent that note, Clem. Fellows's clerk told me you asked after my lodgings. I guessed the rest."
replace.with:
"I meant to tell you not to follow me to Rochester," I said. "I burned the note. This is London. That is different."

He gave a short laugh that was not amusement. "Venn sent a boy to my door with the hour and the stairs, Clem. He said you would come, and I had better."

replace.find: When you came, I forged a bill to pay the nurse and keep it quiet. Fellows's old master found me out. I was tried at Maidstone and sent across the sea."
replace.with: When you came, I forged a bill to pay the nurse and keep it quiet. Fellows's old master found me out. I was tried at Maidstone and lay years in the hulks off Chatham. I broke out once, the autumn you were fourteen, and they took me again at Gravesend and sent me across the sea."

replace.find: I paid what I could from Sydney through Fellows, for you and for the Leggatt boy too, because his father shod my mare the night I ran and would take no coin. Debts grow weeds if you leave them."
replace.with:
I paid what I could from Sydney through Fellows, for you and for the Leggatt boy too, because the boy fed me the night I ran and his father struck off my iron and would take no coin. Debts grow weeds if you leave them."

I saw the back door at Sallow House, the lantern blown half out, a thin man eating like a dog with iron at his ankle, and Hester's hand shaking as she gave the bread.

replace.find: We walked back along the Embankment in silence.
replace.with: We walked back up through the Temple lanes in silence.

replace.find: In Cursitor Street his lodging was one room over a stationer's, clean and spare, with a cot and a table and a shelf of ledgers and a window that looked onto a wall. On the table lay a stack of letters tied with blue thread, in my own hand returned unopened, and beside them a smaller bundle in his hand, addressed to me and never sent because I had forbidden him to write except through Fellows.
replace.with: His lodging over the tailor's was one room, clean and spare, with a cot and a table and a shelf of ledgers and a window that looked onto a wall. On the table lay a bundle tied with tailor's tape, in his hand, addressed to me and never sent, because Fellows allowed him one letter a month and he had written a great many more.

replace.find:
"You kept them," he said, nodding at the blue thread. "All these years."

"I kept everything. The stone. The April letter. I never read them."
replace.with:
"Did you keep the others?" he said. "The ones I sent."

"I kept everything. The stone. The April letter. Every one after the second, with its seal whole. I never read them."

replace.find: Joby pushed the smaller bundle toward me.
replace.with: Joby pushed the bundle toward me.

replace.find: I untied the thread with fingers that would not steady. The first letter was dated April, in his clerk's careful hand,
replace.with: I untied the tape with fingers that would not steady. The first was dated the night of Lady Ashcombe's ball, in his clerk's careful hand,

replace.find: I had read it four times in his lodging while the kettle cooled.
replace.with: I had broken its seal at last that night in Portman Square, with the rest of the box spilled across my counterpane, and read it until the candle drowned.

replace.find: for the walk to Half Moon Street,
replace.with: for the walk to Portman Square,

replace.find: The mist came up from the rhynes in thin ribbons
replace.with: The mist came up from the dykes in thin ribbons

replace.find: Dust lay upon the wedding table in the parlour,
replace.with: Dust lay upon the wedding table in the morning room,

replace.find: Now I knew the shape of irons. Venn had shown me his hands upon the river, and the constables had shouted after a returned man. I knew what twenty years will do to a mark, how it pales and stays.
replace.with: Now I looked at them and wondered what else she had carried in silence under those cuffs. I knew what twenty years will do to a mark, how it pales and stays.

replace.find: I have prayed for that ship every night since you were three days old.
replace.with: I have prayed for that man every night since you were three days old.

replace.find: how she had walked out with a clerk who copied for Mr Fellows and promised marriage, how Miss Sallow had turned her off when her state showed and then taken her back after the birth, on condition the child be called a distant cousin's orphan and Hester never claim her.
replace.with: how she had walked out with the young smith who mended Miss Sallow's grates and married him in secret at Frindsbury, how Miss Sallow had turned her off when her state showed and then taken her back after the birth, on condition the child be called a foundling taken in charity and Hester never claim her.

replace.find: But I had not been a child in London, dancing all night with Sir Roderick Harle while Joby stood by the wall in his too new coat, tugging his cravat. I had chosen that cruelty grown, to punish them both, and hated myself through every quadrille.
replace.with: But I had not been a child in London, dancing all night with Sir Roderick Harle while Joby stood by the wall in his too new coat, tugging his cravat. I had chosen that cruelty grown, to punish us both, and hated myself through every set.

replace.find: I stopped every clock that night for you, that time should not take you as it took my youth.
replace.with: I would have started every clock that night for you, if I had remembered how to begin again.

replace.find: Her work, paid quarterly through Fellows, no thanks desired.
replace.with: Not her work, as he had believed, but my father's, paid quarterly through Fellows, no thanks desired.

replace.find: I had danced all night with Harle while Joby stood by the wall tugging his cravat, and every turn of the dance had sickened me. That debt stood first.
replace.with: That debt stood first.

replace.find: I will see him in the parlour and finish it.
replace.with: I will see him in the morning room and finish it.

replace.find: as every clock in Sallow House had stood for thirty years since the packet sailed for Barbados without its bride.
replace.with: as every clock in Sallow House had stood for forty years since the packet sailed for Barbados without its bride.

replace.find: Its hands had not moved since I was lifted crying from the next room while Hester lay ill after my birth.
replace.with: Its hands had not moved since the morning her bridegroom sailed, long before I was lifted crying from the next room while Hester lay ill after my birth.

replace.find: He was shown to the parlour where the wedding table still stood
replace.with: He was shown to the morning room where the wedding table still stood

replace.find: Let him see what keeping a slight for thirty years looks like.
replace.with: Let him see what keeping a slight for forty years looks like.

replace.find: “I am twenty four and I know my own mind at last.
replace.with: “I am twenty and I know my own mind at last.

replace.find: Hester came to the parlour door with her cap straight
replace.with: Hester came to the morning room door with her cap straight

replace.find: My dear Clemency, I have waited long enough to write plain. I do not want a fine lady. I want you, if you ever want anything.
replace.with: My dear Clemency, I only ask that you should once tell me plain what would please you, and I will do it if it is in my power.

replace.find: When I was twenty two I danced with Harle to make you smart, and I hated myself through every quadrille. I kept every letter you wrote in a locked box and read none till last week, because I was afraid to want anything.
replace.with: This spring I danced all night with Harle to make you smart, and was sick of myself before the supper bell. I kept every letter you wrote in a locked box, and after the first two I broke no seal till this week, because I was afraid to want anything.

notes: Retitled 7 chapters (three were 'The Convict's Letter'); fixed Silas Venn's timeline so he is the ch2 marsh convict (hulks, escape, 1826 transport) and Hester married him, not a clerk; untangled the letters (read first two, rest sealed; ch6 lodging bundle; one April letter text); aligned ages to 20/22 and forty years of stopped clocks; Portman Square, Temple lodgings, no Embankment, dykes not rhynes; the clocks stopped at the jilting. Kept the compressed 1832 timeline rather than rewriting to the brief's 1835-36 dates.
